questions.stem:
A newborn born at 38 weeks is small for gestational age with marked microcephaly. Examination shows a scattered petechial rash and an enlarged liver and spleen. Platelet count is 48,000/microL (150,000 to 450,000) and hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL (14 to 22). Head ultrasound shows calcifications lining the ventricles. A hearing screen is abnormal in one ear. The mother had normal prenatal labs and no known illness in pregnancy.

Which test is the best way to confirm the most likely diagnosis?
choices: Viral PCR on urine or saliva within the first 3 weeks of life
Specific IgM on cord blood sent to a specialty reference laboratory
Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) testing on the infant's serum
Fetal blood sampling for PCR at 18 weeks in a later pregnancy
Heterophile antibody testing on the infant's serum

explain.html:
Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the most common intrauterine infection: 1 to 2% of US newborns are infected and about 10% of those are affected at birth. Affected infants show growth restriction, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia with petechiae, encephalitis and pneumonitis. The comparison chart's CMV signature is microcephaly, periventricular calcifications, deafness (typically unilateral) and thrombocytopenia with petechiae. Diagnosis is CMV PCR on urine or saliva in the first 3 weeks of life, which is 93 to 100% sensitive and 100% specific; after that window a positive result could reflect infection after birth.

This baby has marked microcephaly, calcifications lining the ventricles, petechiae with a platelet count of 48,000, a big liver and spleen and a one-sided hearing loss. Normal prenatal labs fit, since most maternal CMV goes unnoticed, so early urine or saliva PCR is the confirming test.
explain.table:
Congenital CMVCongenital toxoplasmosis
Head sizeMicrocephalyHydrocephalus
CalcificationsPeriventricularIntracranial, scattered
EyeNot the lead findingChorioretinitis (most frequent)
HearingUnilateral lossNot the clue
Confirm withUrine or saliva PCR in first 3 weeksNewborn IgM, then specialty lab
why: Newborn IgM sent to a specialty lab is the path for congenital toxoplasmosis, not CMV.
RPR screens for syphilis, whose clues are a palm and sole rash, snuffles and periostitis.
Fetal blood sampling at 18 weeks is a prenatal test for toxoplasmosis and cannot diagnose this baby now.
Heterophile antibody testing is not part of the congenital CMV workup.
explain.takeaway: Congenital CMV, the most common intrauterine infection, causes microcephaly, periventricular calcifications, petechiae and hearing loss and is confirmed by urine or saliva PCR in the first 3 weeks of life.

explain.objective: Review clinical signs and symptoms seen in newborns with congenital Cytomegalovirus

questions.stem:
A 2-week-old boy has an enlarging head circumference and poor feeding. Head CT shows dilated lateral ventricles with scattered calcifications throughout the brain tissue. Retinal examination shows bilateral lesions with dense central pigment surrounded by a pale ring. Urine CMV PCR is negative. His mother is a first-time gardener who works in her vegetable beds without gloves and changes the litter box for two outdoor cats.

Which organism is most likely responsible, and how did the mother most likely acquire it?
choices: Cytomegalovirus, from contact with saliva of young children
Rubella virus, from respiratory droplets of an unvaccinated contact
Listeria monocytogenes, from soft cheese or deli meat
Treponema pallidum, from sexual contact during the pregnancy
Toxoplasma gondii, from oocysts in cat feces in soil or the litter box

explain.html:
Congenital toxoplasmosis has a classic triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications, though only 10 to 30% of infants show all three. Chorioretinitis is the most frequent finding (85 to 92%), and the retinal lesions have dense central pigment surrounded by a pale ring. Other findings include petechiae, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly and occasionally microcephaly. Risk factors are owning outdoor cats and cleaning the litter box, gardening and soil contact, unwashed produce and undercooked meat, which accounts for about half of US cases.

This baby has an enlarging head with dilated ventricles, scattered calcifications and bilateral pigmented retinal scars, and his urine CMV PCR is negative. His mother gardens bare-handed and changes the litter of outdoor cats, so Toxoplasma gondii from oocysts in cat feces is the answer. CMV would give microcephaly with periventricular calcifications instead.
why: CMV causes microcephaly with periventricular calcifications, and his urine CMV PCR is negative.
Congenital rubella causes cataracts, deafness and heart defects, not hydrocephalus with chorioretinitis.
Listeria causes neonatal sepsis or meningitis, not a triad of hydrocephalus, calcifications and retinal scars.
Congenital syphilis presents with a palm and sole rash, snuffles and periostitis.
explain.takeaway: Congenital toxoplasmosis presents with chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications and is acquired from cat feces, soil or undercooked meat.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Distinguish the clinical findings of congenital Toxoplasmosis from those of infants with other congenital infections

questions.stem:
Two pregnant women in the same clinic have documented primary Toxoplasma gondii infection. Woman 1 seroconverted at 10 weeks' gestation. Woman 2 seroconverted at 32 weeks' gestation. Neither has a history of earlier infection. A student asks how the two pregnancies compare in the chance that the fetus becomes infected and in how severely an infected infant is likely to be affected.

Which comparison is correct?
choices: Woman 1 has the higher transmission risk and a more severely affected infant if infected
Woman 2 has the higher transmission risk and a more severely affected infant if infected
Woman 2 has the lower transmission risk but a more severely affected infant if infected
Woman 1 has the lower transmission risk but the more severely affected infant if infected
Both have the same transmission risk, because each is a primary infection

explain.html:
For congenital infections, timing is everything: both the chance of transmission and the severity of fetal disease depend on when the mother is infected. For toxoplasmosis, transmission risk rises with gestational age, about 15% in the first trimester, 30% in the second and 60% in the third. Severity runs the other way: infection early in pregnancy most often produces a severely affected infant, because it hits the fetus during organ development. Whether the maternal infection is primary or a reactivation also matters, with primary infection carrying more risk.

Both women have primary infections, so timing separates them. Woman 1, at 10 weeks, is less likely to transmit, but an infected fetus would likely be badly affected. Woman 2, at 32 weeks, is more likely to transmit, usually with milder disease.
explain.table:
Trimester of maternal infectionTransmission riskSeverity if infected
FirstAbout 15%Most severe
SecondAbout 30%Intermediate
ThirdAbout 60%Usually milder
why: First-trimester infection has the lowest transmission risk, not the highest.
Late infection transmits more often but usually causes milder disease, not more severe.
Late infection carries the higher transmission risk, and it is usually the milder disease.
Transmission depends on gestational age, not only on whether the infection is primary.
explain.takeaway: In maternal toxoplasmosis, transmission risk rises with gestational age while fetal disease is most severe when infection occurs early.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Distinguish the clinical findings of congenital Toxoplasmosis from those of infants with other congenital infections

questions.stem:
A 27-year-old woman at 14 weeks' gestation has new fatigue and swollen neck lymph nodes. Serology shows Toxoplasma IgG and IgM, both negative on a sample stored from before pregnancy, so this is a new primary infection. Fetal ultrasound is normal, and amniotic fluid PCR is planned for later in pregnancy. Her obstetrician starts a drug right away and explains what it is expected to do.

Which of the following best describes the purpose of this drug?
choices: It treats a fetus that is already infected and reverses brain injury
It lowers the chance that the parasite crosses to the fetus
It clears bradyzoite cysts from the mother's brain and eye
It replaces pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine for the newborn
It prevents reactivation of a latent infection later in life

explain.html:
Management of toxoplasmosis in pregnancy works in steps. Ultrasound may show growth restriction, hydrocephalus, calcifications or ascites, and at about 18 weeks fetal blood or amniotic fluid PCR can look for fetal infection. Spiramycin, given after an acute maternal infection, reduces transmission to the fetus by about 50%. It does not treat a fetus that is already infected. An infected newborn is treated instead with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine for at least a year.

This woman at 14 weeks has a documented new primary infection and a normal ultrasound, so the drug started right away is spiramycin, aimed at keeping the parasite from crossing. Amniotic fluid PCR later in pregnancy is planned precisely because spiramycin cannot fix an infection that has already reached the fetus.
explain.table:
DrugGiven toPurpose
SpiramycinPregnant woman with acute infectionCuts transmission to the fetus by about 50%; does not treat an infected fetus
Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazineInfected newborn, at least 1 yearTreats tachyzoites; improves neurologic, eye and hearing outcomes
why: Spiramycin does not treat a fetus that is already infected, and no drug reverses brain injury.
Neither spiramycin nor pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine clears bradyzoite cysts, which persist in the eye and brain.
Infected newborns get pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine; spiramycin is a pregnancy drug.
Spiramycin is given to cut fetal transmission, not to prevent later reactivation in the mother.
explain.takeaway: Spiramycin given after acute maternal toxoplasmosis cuts transmission to the fetus by about 50% but does not treat an already infected fetus.

explain.objective: Distinguish the clinical findings of congenital Toxoplasmosis from those of infants with other congenital infections

questions.stem:
A 16-day-old girl is evaluated for poor growth. She was born at term to a first-time mother who had several days of low-grade fever and cough in the late first trimester; the mother's immunity status was never confirmed before pregnancy. The infant has a continuous murmur, cloudy lenses in both eyes, an enlarged liver and spleen, and failed hearing screens in both ears. Echocardiogram shows a patent ductus arteriosus. Head CT shows two small calcifications.

Which congenital infection is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection
Congenital toxoplasmosis
Congenital varicella syndrome
Congenital syphilis
Congenital rubella syndrome

explain.html:
Congenital rubella syndrome has transient findings (lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, poor growth, bone marrow involvement, jaundice) and permanent findings centered on the heart, eye, brain and ear. Cardiac lesions appear in over half of affected infants: patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary arterial stenosis and pulmonary valve stenosis. The eye shows retinopathy and cataracts, and deafness, usually bilateral, is the most common finding. The range of defects is inversely related to gestational age at maternal infection: first-trimester infection most often gives multiple anomalies, while infection after 12 weeks may leave only deafness or retinopathy.

This baby's mother had a febrile illness in the late first trimester, her immunity was never confirmed, and the infant has cloudy lenses, bilateral failed hearing screens, a PDA and a big liver and spleen. A couple of small calcifications do not change the call, since the cardiac, eye and bilateral ear findings together are rubella.
explain.table:
Timing of maternal rubellaTypical outcome
First trimesterHighest risk, multiple anomalies (heart, eye, ear)
After 12 weeksOften deafness or retinopathy only
why: CMV gives microcephaly, periventricular calcifications and petechiae with one-sided hearing loss, not cataracts and a PDA.
Toxoplasmosis causes chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and calcifications, not cataracts with a PDA.
Congenital varicella causes limb hypoplasia and skin scars along with cataracts, and no heart lesion.
Congenital syphilis causes a palm and sole rash, snuffles and periostitis.
explain.takeaway: Congenital rubella causes cataracts, bilateral deafness and heart defects such as PDA and pulmonary stenosis, with the most anomalies after first-trimester infection.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Review the clinical manifestations of congenital Rubella syndrome

questions.stem:
A 4-week-old boy is brought in for a persistent, blood-tinged nasal discharge and poor feeding. Examination shows a copper-colored maculopapular rash on the palms and soles and an enlarged liver. He cries when his arms are moved, and radiographs show inflammation along the shafts of several long bones. His mother had little prenatal care and had a painless genital sore early in pregnancy that healed on its own.

Which treatment is indicated for this infant?
choices: Ganciclovir
Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine
Varicella-zoster immune globulin
Penicillin
No specific antimicrobial treatment exists

explain.html:
Each TORCH infection has a set of clue findings and its own treatment, and the comparison chart lines them up. Congenital syphilis shows a maculopapular rash on the palms and soles, snuffles and periostitis, and it is treated with penicillin. Toxoplasmosis shows hydrocephalus, calcifications and chorioretinitis and is treated with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine. Rubella shows cataracts, deafness and heart defects and has no specific treatment. CMV shows microcephaly, periventricular calcifications and petechiae and is treated with ganciclovir, and varicella shows limb hypoplasia and scars, with VZIG for a baby whose mother is infected around delivery.

This infant has a blood-tinged persistent nasal discharge, a copper palm and sole rash, a big liver and painful long bones with periostitis, and his mother had a painless genital sore that healed on its own. That is congenital syphilis, so penicillin is the treatment.

ToxoplasmosisHydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications, chorioretinitisPyrimethamine and sulfadiazine
RubellaCataracts, bilateral deafness, heart defects (PDA)None specific

VaricellaLimb hypoplasia, skin scars, cataractsVZIG for the newborn if mother infected around delivery
why: Ganciclovir treats congenital CMV, which presents with microcephaly, periventricular calcifications and petechiae.
Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine treat congenital toxoplasmosis.
Varicella-zoster immune globulin is for a newborn whose mother had varicella around delivery.
No specific treatment is the answer for congenital rubella, not syphilis.
explain.takeaway: Congenital syphilis (palm and sole rash, snuffles, periostitis) is treated with penicillin, while congenital rubella has no specific treatment.

questions.stem:
A term newborn develops grunting, tachypnea, poor perfusion and a temperature of 38.4 C (101.1 F) two hours after a vaginal delivery. Membranes had been ruptured for 22 hours before birth, and the mother received no antibiotics during labor. Blood culture grows facultative Gram-positive cocci in chains that are beta-hemolytic. Chest radiograph shows diffuse bilateral opacities.

Which maternal factor was the most important determinant of this infection?
choices: Presence of the organism in the maternal genital tract at delivery
Maternal ingestion of soft cheese or deli meat during pregnancy
Primary maternal infection acquired in the first trimester
Contact with cat feces while the mother was gardening
Maternal bloodstream infection that seeded the placenta before delivery

explain.html:
Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is a facultative Gram-positive coccus, and the presence of GBS in the maternal genital tract at delivery is the most important determinant of early-onset neonatal infection. About 15 to 40% of women are colonized, and infants acquire the organism by the ascending route or during delivery, about 50% of the time when no intrapartum antibiotics are given. Prolonged rupture of membranes and preterm delivery add risk. Early-onset disease (under 7 days, median onset 1 hour) presents as septicemia, pneumonia and meningitis, while late-onset disease (7 to 89 days) is bacteremia without a focus, meningitis or bone and joint infection.

This baby was septic with pneumonia 2 hours after birth, with 22 hours of ruptured membranes, no intrapartum antibiotics and beta-hemolytic Gram-positive cocci in chains. The mother's colonization at delivery is what made this happen.
explain.table:
Early-onset GBSLate-onset GBS
AgeUnder 7 days (median 1 hour)7 to 89 days (median 27 days)
PictureSepticemia, pneumonia, meningitisBacteremia without focus, meningitis (often serotype III), bone and joint infection
why: Soft cheese and deli meat are sources of Listeria, a Gram-positive rod, not a coccus in chains.
Primary first-trimester infection is the pattern of the TORCH pathogens, not GBS.
Cat feces transmit Toxoplasma, which causes congenital infection, not early-onset sepsis.
Maternal bacteremia that seeds the placenta describes Listeria; GBS comes from genital tract colonization.
explain.takeaway: Maternal genital tract colonization with GBS at delivery is the key determinant of early-onset neonatal sepsis, pneumonia and meningitis.

explain.objective: Describe the bacterial pathogens associated with early onset neonatal infection

questions.stem:
A 6-day-old boy born at 34 weeks after 30 hours of ruptured membranes develops fever, irritability, a bulging fontanelle and poor feeding. His mother had a fever during labor. Cerebrospinal fluid shows many neutrophils and Gram-negative rods, and culture grows a lactose-fermenting organism. Typing shows the isolate carries a particular capsular polysaccharide antigen.

Which virulence factor is most specifically associated with this organism causing neonatal meningitis?
choices: A lipid-rich waxy cell wall rich in mycolic acids
Motility that allows the organism to spread to the placenta
A fusion protein that lets it enter epithelial cells
Beta-hemolysis caused by a secreted toxin
K1 capsular polysaccharide antigen

explain.html:
Three bacterial groups dominate early neonatal infection: GBS, Listeria, and E. coli and other Gram-negative rods. Neonatal bacteremia and meningitis from E. coli look clinically like GBS, and the source is the maternal genital tract. The E. coli strain with the K1 capsular polysaccharide antigen is uniquely associated with neonatal meningitis. Predisposing factors include maternal intrapartum infection, maternal antibiotic use, gestational age under 37 weeks, low birth weight, prolonged rupture of membranes and, among metabolic causes, galactosemia.

This 34-week baby with 30 hours of ruptured membranes and a febrile mother has meningitis with Gram-negative rods that ferment lactose and carry a capsular antigen. That is E. coli, and the K1 capsule is the virulence factor tied to neonatal meningitis.

E. coliGram-negative rodMaternal genital tract; K1 capsule linked to meningitis
why: A waxy, mycolic acid wall describes mycobacteria, not a lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod.
Motility with spread to the placenta describes Listeria, a Gram-positive rod.
A fusion protein for cell entry describes RSV, a virus.
Beta-hemolysis describes group B Streptococcus, a Gram-positive coccus.
explain.takeaway: E. coli with the K1 capsular antigen is uniquely associated with neonatal meningitis, with risks including prematurity, prolonged rupture of membranes and maternal intrapartum infection.

questions.stem:
Two women deliver infants on the same day. Woman 1 was CMV seronegative at her first prenatal visit and seroconverted during the second trimester. Woman 2 has been CMV seropositive since adolescence, and PCR showed viral shedding in her urine late in pregnancy. Both infants are tested at birth. A student asks which infant is more likely to have symptomatic disease and why.

Which of the following is the best answer?
choices: Woman 2's infant, because reactivated virus is more virulent
Both equally, because maternal IgG does not cross the placenta to protect them
Woman 2's infant, because shedding late in pregnancy reaches the fetus
Woman 1's infant, because primary maternal infection more often causes fetal disease
Neither, because CMV causes disease only in immunocompromised hosts

explain.html:
The risk a maternal infection poses to the fetus depends on whether it is primary or secondary. A primary maternal infection, acquired during pregnancy in a woman with no prior immunity, is more likely to cause infection and disease in the fetus. A secondary infection, a reactivation of an old infection, may still infect the fetus but is usually less likely to cause disease or symptoms. Part of the protection comes from pre-existing maternal immunity, including IgG that crosses the placenta in the last trimester.

Woman 1 was seronegative and seroconverted in the second trimester, a primary infection, so her infant is at higher risk of symptomatic congenital CMV. Woman 2 has been seropositive since adolescence, so her late shedding is a reactivation, and her infant may be infected but is less likely to be sick.
why: Reactivated virus is not more virulent; reactivation is less likely to cause fetal disease.
Maternal IgG does cross the placenta, in the last trimester.
Shedding from a reactivation can reach the fetus but usually causes less disease than a primary infection.
CMV is the most common congenital infection and clearly causes disease in fetuses.
explain.takeaway: Primary maternal infection during pregnancy is more likely to cause fetal disease than reactivation of a prior infection.

questions.stem:
A term newborn is small for gestational age and has an enlarged liver and spleen. The mother had a mild febrile illness with swollen neck lymph nodes in the second trimester. Serology for a parasitic congenital pathogen is sent on both:

[[labs 0]]

Which result best establishes that the newborn himself is infected?
choices: The newborn's IgG, because it matches the mother's high titer
The newborn's IgM, because it does not cross the placenta
The mother's IgM, because it proves a recent primary infection
The mother's IgG, because it proves infection before pregnancy
The newborn's IgG, because the fetus makes IgG by mid-gestation

explain.html:
The newborn's antibody profile follows from what crosses the placenta. A baby has no IgG of its own at birth; the IgG present is the mother's, transferred across the placenta in the last trimester. IgM does not cross the placenta, and the newborn can make it, reaching adult levels by 2 to 3 months. So a newborn IgG that matches the mother's titer tells you only about her, while a specific IgM in the newborn shows the baby's own immune system met the organism in utero. That is why screening IgM in the newborn is the diagnostic step for congenital toxoplasmosis, with a positive result sent on to a specialty lab.

Here mother and baby have the same high IgG titer, which is simply hers, and both are IgM positive. Only the newborn's IgM establishes that the baby is infected.
explain.table:
Antibody in the newbornSourceMeaning
IgGMother, across the placenta in the last trimesterReflects maternal exposure only
IgMThe newborn itself (does not cross the placenta)The baby was infected
why: A newborn IgG equal to the mother's is transplacental maternal antibody and says nothing about the baby.
Maternal IgM supports a recent infection in the mother but cannot show that the fetus was infected.
Maternal IgG shows she was infected at some time, not that the baby was.
The fetus does not make meaningful IgG; newborn IgG at birth is the mother's.
explain.takeaway: Newborn IgG at birth is maternal, crossing the placenta in the last trimester, so a specific IgM in the newborn is what proves congenital infection.

questions.stem:
A 5-day-old girl has confirmed symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus infection with hearing loss. Her team chooses an oral drug, given for 6 months, that the intestine converts to its active parent compound. A pharmacology student asks why the drug is relatively selective for infected cells and what kind of viral change could make it fail.

Which statement best answers the student?
choices: It needs a viral thymidine kinase for activation; resistance comes from loss of a host transporter
It binds viral neuraminidase in infected cells; resistance comes from accumulated point mutations in the viral hemagglutinin
It needs a viral kinase for its first phosphorylation; resistance is from mutations in that kinase or the polymerase
It blocks viral uncoating in infected cells; resistance comes from mutations in the capsid protein
It is activated by host kinases only; resistance comes from increased host enzyme production

explain.html:
Symptomatic congenital CMV is treated with IV ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir, and a randomized trial showed that 6 months of valganciclovir improved hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes to at least age 2. Valganciclovir is the L-valyl ester of ganciclovir, converted to ganciclovir by the intestine. Ganciclovir is first phosphorylated by a viral kinase encoded by CMV gene UL97, then by human cellular kinases to ganciclovir triphosphate. The triphosphate competitively inhibits deoxyguanosine triphosphate incorporation and preferentially inhibits viral DNA polymerase over cellular polymerases.

Because the first step needs the viral enzyme, active drug builds up mainly in infected cells, which answers the student's first question. Resistance comes from mutations in the UL97 phosphotransferase (no activation) or the UL54-encoded DNA polymerase (altered target).
why: Activation does use a viral kinase, but resistance comes from UL97 or UL54 mutations, not loss of a host transporter.
Neuraminidase and hemagglutinin are influenza proteins, not CMV targets.
Ganciclovir inhibits viral DNA polymerase; it does not block uncoating.
Activation by host kinases alone would give no selectivity for infected cells, and resistance is from viral mutations.
explain.takeaway: Valganciclovir is converted to ganciclovir, which is first phosphorylated by the CMV UL97 kinase and inhibits viral DNA polymerase; resistance arises from UL97 or UL54 mutations.

explain.objective: Review clinical signs and symptoms seen in newborns with congenital Cytomegalovirus

rows.why: Activation does use a viral kinase, but resistance comes from UL97 or UL54 mutations, not loss of a host transporter.
rows.if_right: a drug whose resistance is caused by reduced uptake into the cell

rows.why: Neuraminidase and hemagglutinin are influenza proteins, not CMV targets.
rows.if_right: an oral sialic acid analog given for influenza

rows.why: Ganciclovir inhibits viral DNA polymerase; it does not block uncoating.
rows.if_right: a drug that stops the viral genome from being released after entry

rows.why: Activation by host kinases alone would give no selectivity for infected cells, and resistance is from viral mutations.
rows.if_right: a drug that is equally active in infected and uninfected cells

questions.stem:
An infant with confirmed congenital toxoplasmosis is started on two drugs that will be continued for at least 1 year, along with a vitamin to prevent a blood count problem caused by one of them. At 6 weeks the infant develops hives from the other drug. The parents ask whether, once a full year of treatment is completed, the infection will be gone for good.

Which of the following is the best answer to the parents?
choices: Yes, because the drugs kill all forms of the parasite in the brain and eye
Yes, because treatment that began at birth prevents any new tissue cysts from ever forming anywhere
No, because the drugs act on tachyzoites but do not clear bradyzoites in the eye and brain
No, because the parasite rapidly becomes resistant to both drugs during therapy
No, because the parasite persists in the gut and is shed for years afterward

explain.html:
Infected newborns with toxoplasmosis are treated with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine for at least a year, which improves neurologic, cognitive, eye and hearing outcomes compared with untreated children. Each drug has its own adverse effect: pyrimethamine causes neutropenia, so folic acid is given with it, and sulfadiazine causes hives and rash. These drugs are active against tachyzoites, the actively dividing form. They do not effectively eradicate bradyzoites in tissue cysts of the eye and central nervous system.

That is the answer to the parents: even after a full year, cysts can remain, and late recurrence of eye and brain disease after treatment ends is a known risk, so the child needs ongoing follow-up. The hives at 6 weeks fit sulfadiazine, and the vitamin is the folic acid given with pyrimethamine.
why: The drugs act on tachyzoites but do not clear bradyzoites from the eye and brain.
Tissue cysts form during fetal infection, before treatment begins at birth.
Resistance is not the reason for late recurrence; persistence of bradyzoites is.
The concern is cysts in the eye and brain, not shedding from the gut.
explain.takeaway: Congenital toxoplasmosis is treated with pyrimethamine (plus folic acid for neutropenia) and sulfadiazine, which kill tachyzoites but not bradyzoites, so late eye and CNS recurrence can occur.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Distinguish the clinical findings of congenital Toxoplasmosis from those of infants with other congenital infections

rows.why: The drugs act on tachyzoites but do not clear bradyzoites from the eye and brain.
rows.if_right: a drug that eradicates every form of the parasite, including tissue cysts

rows.why: Tissue cysts form during fetal infection, before treatment begins at birth.
rows.if_right: an infection caught and treated before the parasite reached the fetus

rows.why: Resistance is not the reason for late recurrence; persistence of bradyzoites is.
rows.if_right: a cavitary TB patient given a single drug, which selects resistant mutants

rows.why: The concern is cysts in the eye and brain, not shedding from the gut.
rows.if_right: a household cat, whose feces carry the infective stage into litter boxes and soil

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old woman at 32 weeks' gestation had 4 days of fever, headache, backache, nausea and diarrhea, then went into premature labor. She reports eating ready-to-eat deli salads and unpasteurized soft cheese several times in the past month. Her infant is lethargic, with temperature instability. Placental culture and the infant's blood and cerebrospinal fluid cultures grow a motile Gram-positive rod.

Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate for the infant?
choices: Ganciclovir for 6 weeks
Ampicillin combined with gentamicin
Pyrimethamine combined with sulfadiazine
Spiramycin given until 1 year of age
Rifampin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide

explain.html:
Listeria monocytogenes is a Gram-positive, motile rod found widely in the environment, and its food sources include soft cheeses, ready-to-eat salads, processed deli meats and hot dogs. Infected mothers may have an influenza-like illness with fever, headache, backache, nausea and diarrhea, or be bacteremic without symptoms. Maternal bacteremia infects the placenta and fetus, and these mothers may go into premature labor. Early-onset neonatal listeriosis (under 5 days) is usually sepsis or meningitis, and the workup includes blood, cerebrospinal fluid and placental cultures.

This mother had a flu-like illness after deli salads and unpasteurized soft cheese, delivered at 32 weeks, and the placenta, blood and CSF all grew a motile Gram-positive rod. Treatment is ampicillin combined with gentamicin.
why: Ganciclovir is an antiviral for CMV and has no activity against a bacterium.
Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine treat congenital toxoplasmosis.
Spiramycin is given to pregnant women to reduce toxoplasma transmission, not to treat neonatal sepsis.
These are tuberculosis drugs and do not treat neonatal listeriosis.
explain.takeaway: Neonatal listeriosis follows a maternal flu-like illness from soft cheese or deli foods, often with preterm labor, and is treated with ampicillin plus gentamicin.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe the bacterial pathogens associated with early onset neonatal infection

rows.why: Ganciclovir is an antiviral for CMV and has no activity against a bacterium.
rows.if_right: a newborn with symptomatic congenital CMV

rows.why: Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine treat congenital toxoplasmosis.
rows.if_right: a newborn with hydrocephalus, calcifications and chorioretinitis

rows.why: Spiramycin is given to pregnant women to reduce toxoplasma transmission, not to treat neonatal sepsis.
rows.if_right: a pregnant woman with newly acquired toxoplasmosis

rows.why: These are tuberculosis drugs and do not treat neonatal listeriosis.
rows.if_right: an infant with tuberculosis
